title: Maharaja Yayati's lust and renunciation
summary: Yayati, cursed by Sukracarya with premature old age, borrowed the youth of his youngest son Puru and enjoyed for a thousand years. At last he saw that desire is never satisfied by enjoyment, like a fire fed with butter, returned the youth and went to the forest to worship Krsna.
lesson: Enjoyment feeds desire; it cannot end it.
useFor: Use after describing the 'one more' cycle of craving: even a king with a thousand years of pleasure concluded it does not work.

title: Ajamila and the holy name
summary: Ajamila was a learned brahmana who fell into a sinful life. At death he called out his youngest son's name, Narayana, and Lord Visnu's messengers stopped the messengers of Yama. He was given a chance, renounced everything and became a devotee.
lesson: The holy name has power even when chanted imperfectly; it also asks for a serious change of life afterwards.
useFor: Use for the power of the name, then add the second half: he did not go back to sin.

title: Prahlada under pressure
summary: Five-year-old Prahlada told his father Hiranyakasipu that devotion to Visnu is the best education. The enraged king tried to have him killed in many ways, yet Prahlada stayed unharmed and unafraid, and the Lord appeared as Nrsimha.
lesson: Faith grounded in the Lord stays calm when everyone opposes it.
useFor: Use for peer pressure and fear of opposition at home or college: a child stood firm.

title: Prahlada teaches his classmates
summary: In the teachers' absence Prahlada gathered his demoniac classmates and told them to begin devotional service from childhood, because human life is rare, uncertain and short. His friends listened and were moved.
lesson: Do not postpone the real purpose of life; start young.
useFor: Use for 'I will do spiritual life later': the question is who guarantees later.

title: Dhruva's determination
summary: Insulted by his stepmother, five-year-old Dhruva went to the forest to see the Lord. Following Narada's instruction he practised severe austerity and saw Visnu; he then said he was fully satisfied and wanted no boon.
lesson: Determination for the right goal ends in more than the original wish.
useFor: Use for focus and resolve; and for how motive changes in the company of the Lord.

title: Bharata Maharaja and the deer
summary: Bharata Maharaja had retired to the forest and worshipped the Lord, but he became attached to an orphan deer. At death he thought of the deer and took birth as one, with memory of his past.
lesson: What fills the mind at death shapes the next life; small attachments grow.
useFor: Use for attachment and its price: even a sincere renunciant can fall through a pet.

title: Bharata Maharaja gives up his kingdom
summary: Bharata, the emperor for whom India is named, gave up his wife, children, friends and kingdom, which are hard to give up, like cast-off stool, to worship the Lord. His dear devotee-ancestor is the real meaning of 'Bharata'.
lesson: Real greatness is the ability to give up for the Lord.
useFor: Use for 'India vs Bharat' and for what renunciation means in practice.

title: Citraketu: a son, a loss, a lesson
summary: Citraketu, a king with many wives and no child, was given a son by the sage Angira; the child died, apparently poisoned by a jealous co-wife. Narada showed him that the child was not really his, and Citraketu turned to the Lord. Later he bore Parvati's curse without anger.
lesson: Family ties are real in duty but temporary in truth; devotees of Narayana fear nothing.
useFor: Use for grief and attachment to relatives, and for tolerating a curse.

title: Vrtrasura's prayer
summary: Vrtrasura, killer of brahmanas and Indra's enemy, faced Indra in battle undaunted, talking of devotion even as he fought. He prayed not for heaven but to be the servant of the Lord's servants, like unfledged birds who await their mother.
lesson: The devotee wants service, not position; fear of death does not touch him.
useFor: Use for fearlessness and for the service mood.

title: Gajendra's surrender
summary: The king of elephants was seized by a crocodile and strove for a thousand years. When his strength was gone he decided to take shelter of the Lord and prayed, and the Lord came and delivered him.
lesson: In real helplessness, surrender is the only intelligent act.
useFor: Use for stress and helplessness: when all your own effort has failed, whom do you call?

title: Kunti's prayers
summary: Queen Kunti, who had been saved from poison, fire and the insult of the assembly, prayed to Krsna that calamities should come again, for in them she could see Him. She asked that her attachment to relatives be cut and her mind flow to Him like the Ganga.
lesson: Difficulty can be welcome when it turns us to the Lord.
useFor: Use for 'why do bad things happen': a devotee's answer.

title: Pariksit's curse and the Bhagavatam
summary: King Pariksit, thirsty and tired, disrespected a meditating sage; the sage's son cursed him to die in seven days. Pariksit accepted it as a blessing, sat on the Ganga bank and heard the Bhagavatam from Sukadeva Gosvami.
lesson: Death is certain; the wise use the time to hear.
useFor: Use for time and death: what would you do with seven days?

title: Narada's previous life
summary: Narada was in a previous life the son of a maidservant who served wandering sages during the rainy season. He ate the remnants of their food, heard their talks and by their mercy gained a taste for the Lord; later, after his mother's death, he went out and heard the Lord's voice.
lesson: Humble service and hearing to saintly people can change a life.
useFor: Use for association and service: a child with no qualification.

title: Haridasa Thakura and the prostitute
summary: Ramacandra Khan, envious of Haridasa Thakura, sent a prostitute to disturb his chanting. Haridasa told her to wait until he finished his number; night after night he went on chanting, and by his association she became a pure devotee.
lesson: Steady chanting is stronger than temptation.
useFor: Use for temptation and the purity of the name: the tempter was transformed.

title: Chota Haridasa
summary: Chota Haridasa, a singer in Lord Caitanya's circle, begged rice from an elderly lady devotee at the request of Bhagavan Acarya. Hearing that a renunciant had spoken with a woman, the Lord refused to see him, and Haridasa gave up his body at Prayaga.
lesson: A renunciant's association must be guarded; the Lord's strictness is for our protection.
useFor: Use for brahmacari or sannyasa vows: rules are strict for the sake of the ideal.

title: Raghunatha dasa Gosvami's renunciation
summary: Raghunatha dasa, the son of a very wealthy man, left his family repeatedly until he reached Lord Caitanya at Puri. He lived with extreme simplicity, eating only discarded prasada, and later lived at Radha-kunda in great austerity. Lord Caitanya gave him the instruction: do not talk or hear ordinary talk.
lesson: Renunciation is the fruit of attachment to Krsna.
useFor: Use for 'what real vairagya looks like'.

title: Sanatana Gosvami: 'Who am I?'
summary: Sanatana Gosvami, a minister of the Muslim ruler, gave up his post and met Lord Caitanya at Benares. He asked the Lord 'Who am I, and why do the threefold miseries trouble me?', and the Lord taught him.
lesson: The first real question is about the self.
useFor: Use as an opening: a successful minister asked this question.

title: Amogha, the critic
summary: Amogha, the son-in-law of Sarvabhauma Bhattacarya, criticised the Lord's eating, and was struck by cholera. The Lord revived him and said the brahmana's heart is meant to be the Lord's seat and should be kept clean of envy; Amogha then chanted and became a devotee.
lesson: Fault-finding pollutes the heart; forgiveness cleans it.
useFor: Use for fault-finding and envy.

title: Sarvabhauma Bhattacarya's change
summary: Sarvabhauma, a famed scholar of Nyaya and Advaita, first pitied the young sannyasi Caitanya, then lost an argument on the atmarama verse and was shown the six-handed form. He became a great devotee.
lesson: Learning without humility blocks the heart; the Lord's mercy opens it.
useFor: Use for pride of knowledge.

title: The brahmana of Avanti
summary: A rich, miserly brahmana of Avanti lost his wealth and was despised by family and friends. He took sannyasa, tolerated insults from the public, and sang that no person is the cause of his happiness and distress: it is the mind.
lesson: Happiness and distress are mind's reactions; control the mind and tolerate.
useFor: Use for stress, insult, anger.

title: The avadhuta's twenty-four gurus
summary: A wandering avadhuta told King Yadu that he had taken shelter of twenty-four gurus drawn from nature, among them the earth, air, water, fire, python, pigeon and honeybee. A humble seeker learns from everything.
lesson: A humble seeker learns from everyone.
useFor: Use for 'learning from others' and for teaching with simple images.

title: Pingala
summary: Pingala, a courtesan of Videha, waited a whole night for a wealthy customer who never came. She realised that hope for sense gratification is the greatest misery, and that giving it up brings peace and the desire to serve the Lord.
lesson: Giving up expectation is a source of peace.
useFor: Use for stress and craving.

title: Saubhari Muni
summary: The yogi Saubhari, long in austerity under the Yamuna, saw fish mating and desired a wife; he married the fifty daughters of King Mandhata and enjoyed a household of great opulence. In the end, he saw his downfall came from his association and returned to renunciation.
lesson: Even a great yogi can fall by sense desire.
useFor: Use for the danger of sensual association.

title: Ambarisa and Durvasa
summary: Durvasa Muni cursed King Ambarisa over a delay in breaking his fast. The Lord's Sudarsana disc, set to protect Ambarisa, chased Durvasa through the universe; Durvasa was finally forgiven only when Ambarisa asked.
lesson: Offence to a devotee brings trouble; a true devotee does not retaliate.
useFor: Use for Vaisnava aparadha and tolerance.

title: Kardama Muni and Devahuti
summary: Svayambhuva Manu offered his daughter Devahuti to Kardama Muni, who accepted on condition that they would stay together only until a child was born. Devahuti served devotedly; their nine daughters were married and the Lord appeared as their son, Kapila.
lesson: Marriage can be a spiritual partnership.
useFor: Use for ideal grhastha life.

title: Lord Kapila teaches Devahuti
summary: Devahuti asked her son, Lord Kapila, how to be free of material attachment. He taught her that the mind alone is the cause of bondage and liberation, and that pure devotion is the highest path.
lesson: The mind decides bondage or liberation.
useFor: Use for mind control.

title: Rsyasrnga
summary: Romapada, who had no child, accepted Santa, the daughter of his friend Dasaratha, as his own, and she married Rsyasrnga. When the demigods withheld rain, Rsyasrnga was brought from the forest by prostitutes who allured him, and was made priest of the sacrifice.
lesson: Innocence is protected by seclusion; sense contact can disturb it.
useFor: Use for brahmacari discipline.

title: Nalakuvara and Manigriva
summary: The sons of Kuvera, intoxicated with wealth and wine, became shameless. Narada cursed them to be trees; Krsna, as a child, pulled the mortar through the two trees and freed them. They prayed to Him.
lesson: Intoxication of wealth blinds; a curse can be a mercy.
useFor: Use for intoxication and pride.

title: Sudama
summary: Sudama, a poor brahmana and Krsna's schoolmate, visited Dvaraka with a gift of flattened rice. Krsna received him with great love and ate; Sudama came away without asking anything and found his home made opulent.
lesson: Krsna accepts love, not value.
useFor: Use for gratitude and giving what you can.

title: The brahmana wives
summary: Krsna's hungry cowherd friends asked brahmanas performing a sacrifice for food and were refused. The brahmanas' wives, hearing of Krsna, hurried to Him with food despite their husbands' objection, and afterwards the husbands regretted.
lesson: Spontaneous love overcomes ritual pride.
useFor: Use for service attitude and humility.

title: Lord Rama accepts exile
summary: Lord Ramacandra left for fourteen years in the forest to keep his father Dasaratha's promise. Sita and Laksmana followed him.
lesson: Ideal conduct honours a father's word.
useFor: Use for duty to parents.

title: Hanuman's service
summary: In Kimpurusa-varsa, Hanuman continually worships Lord Ramacandra with Sita; the residents sing His glories. Hanuman's prayers speak of a servant's wish.
lesson: A servant's joy is service.
useFor: Use for service attitude.

title: Ravana and Sita
summary: Ravana, the king of Lanka, abducted Sita and was destroyed by Lord Rama. His fall followed from desire for another's wife.
lesson: Lust and pride destroy even the powerful.
useFor: Use for lust and pride.

title: Bhisma's passing
summary: Lying on a bed of arrows, Bhisma waited for the auspicious time to leave his body and instructed Yudhisthira on dharma. At the end, he fixed his mind on Krsna and gave up his body.
lesson: A life of dharma ends with Krsna remembered.
useFor: Use for death and dharma.

title: Draupadi forgives Asvatthama
summary: Asvatthama killed the sleeping sons of Draupadi. When Arjuna brought him bound, Draupadi, though overwhelmed with grief, asked that he be released as a brahmana and the son of a teacher.
lesson: Grief did not turn her into a revenge-seeker.
useFor: Use for anger and forgiveness.

title: Arjuna's collapse and the Gita
summary: On Kurukshetra Arjuna put down his bow, confused about duty, and surrendered to Krsna as a disciple, asking what is best for him.
lesson: Confusion honestly admitted begins wisdom.
useFor: Use for depression and decision.

title: Dhrtarastra quits home
summary: Vidura told his elder brother Dhrtarastra that eternal time was upon him, that his sons and well-wishers were already gone, and that he should leave home. Dhrtarastra left with Gandhari.
lesson: A wise man leaves before death forces him.
useFor: Use for time and attachment.

title: Lord Rsabhadeva's instruction
summary: Lord Rsabhadeva told his hundred sons that the path of liberation is opened by serving highly advanced spiritual persons, and that one who cannot deliver his dependents from birth and death should not become a guru or father.
lesson: Association decides direction.
useFor: Use for association.

title: King Puranjana
summary: King Puranjana, absorbed in his queen and city of nine gates, was swept away by his senses. At death he thought of his wife and took birth as a woman. Narada explained that the story is about every soul.
lesson: The senses and the mind build a city for us and then bind us.
useFor: Use for sense control.

title: The forest of material enjoyment
summary: Jada Bharata told King Rahugana of a merchant who entered a dense forest in search of wealth. Plundered by thieves and harassed by many troubles, he never found rest. Jada Bharata explained that this is the condition of the soul in the material world.
lesson: The search for enjoyment never ends in rest.
useFor: Use for happiness and stress.

title: Lord Krsna subdues Kaliya
summary: The serpent Kaliya poisoned the Yamuna. Krsna danced on his hoods and spared him at the prayer of his wives, who asked what good deed had won him the dust of Krsna's feet.
lesson: Pride is humbled; mercy follows surrender.
useFor: Use for pride.

title: Krsna and Indra: Govardhana
summary: Krsna persuaded the cowherds to stop the sacrifice to Indra. The angry Indra sent a storm; Krsna lifted Govardhana Hill for seven days. Indra's pride was broken.
lesson: Pride in position falls before the Lord.
useFor: Use for whom to worship.

title: Brahma steals the calves
summary: Brahma stole Krsna's calves and cowherd friends to test Him. Krsna expanded Himself into all of them; Brahma, confused, offered prayers beginning with the idea that a devotee sees misfortune as the Lord's mercy.
lesson: Even great minds are small before the Lord.
useFor: Use for suffering as mercy and limits of intelligence.

title: Krsna protects Pariksit in the womb
summary: Uttara, pregnant with Pariksit, ran to Krsna, fearing the fiery brahmastra. Krsna entered her womb and saved the child.
lesson: The Lord protects the surrendered.
useFor: Use for fear.

title: Bali Maharaja and Vamana
summary: Bali Maharaja, though warned by Sukracarya, honoured his promise and gave the Lord Vamana three steps of land. He said he feared cheating a brahmana more than losing everything. The Lord took all, and Bali became His protected devotee.
lesson: Surrender everything and nothing is lost.
useFor: Use for surrender.

title: Mucukunda
summary: King Mucukunda had helped the demigods for ages; he slept in a cave, and his gaze burnt Kalayavana. When Krsna appeared, he asked for no boon but release.
lesson: The tired soul should aspire for service, not enjoyment.
useFor: Use for ambition.

title: Prthu Maharaja asks for ten thousand ears
summary: The ideal king Prthu, offered a boon by the Lord, asked for ten thousand ears so that he could hear the Lord's glories.
lesson: Hearing is the soul's real appetite.
useFor: Use for hearing.

title: Daksa and Siva
summary: Proud Daksa insulted Lord Siva in an assembly; Sati, unable to bear it, gave up her body. Siva's followers destroyed Daksa's sacrifice, and Daksa was later restored and repented.
lesson: Pride and envy toward a devotee destroy.
useFor: Use for aparadha.

title: Jaya and Vijaya's fall
summary: The four Kumaras were stopped at the gate of Vaikuntha by Jaya and Vijaya, and they cursed the gatekeepers to take birth in the material world.
lesson: Offence to saints has quick consequences.
useFor: Use for aparadha.

title: Bhagiratha brings the Ganga
summary: King Bhagiratha, with great austerity, brought Ganga to earth to deliver his ancestors.
lesson: Steady effort can do the impossible.
useFor: Use for determination.

title: Rantideva
summary: After forty-eight days without food, Rantideva gave away his meal to hungry guests. He said he desired no liberation but only to bear the pains of all living beings.
lesson: Compassion is the sign of the real greatness.
useFor: Use for compassion.

title: Visvamitra and Menaka
summary: The great sage Visvamitra's austerity was broken by the apsara Menaka. Their daughter Sakuntala was left in the forest.
lesson: Even great austerity can be undone by sense contact.
useFor: Use for fall from contemplation.

title: Vyasa and Narada
summary: Vyasadeva was dissatisfied after compiling the Vedas. Narada told him that knowledge without devotion to Acyuta is not satisfying, and advised him to describe the Lord's pastimes, which became the Bhagavatam.
lesson: Real satisfaction needs devotion.
useFor: Use for books.

title: Hiranyakasipu's boon
summary: Hiranyakasipu performed severe austerity and asked Brahma for a boon of immortality in various forms. Even with the boon, the Lord ended him in the form of Nrsimha.
lesson: Material plans cannot defeat death.
useFor: Use for ambition and science.

title: The leper Vasudeva
summary: At Kurma-ksetra, Lord Caitanya embraced a leprous brahmana called Vasudeva, and he was cured. Vasudeva, humbly, begged not to be proud.
lesson: The Lord sees the soul, not the illness.
useFor: Use for humility.

title: Rupa Gosvami meets the Lord at Prayaga
summary: Rupa Gosvami, a former minister, met Lord Caitanya at Prayaga. The Lord taught him for ten days, including the seed of devotion given by guru and Krsna.
lesson: Devotion is a seed given by guru and Krsna.
useFor: Use for guru.

title: Madhavendra Puri and Gopala
summary: Madhavendra Puri served the Deity Gopala at Govardhana. When Puri, who asked for nothing, was hungry, Gopala Himself arranged for milk to be brought to him.
lesson: Deity is a person who reciprocates.
useFor: Use for Deity worship.

title: Indra insults Brhaspati
summary: Indra, proud of his opulence, did not rise when Brhaspati, his guru, came, and Brhaspati left. Indra lost the support of his guru and was defeated by the demons.
lesson: Disrespect to elders ruins you.
useFor: Use for dealings with seniors.

title: Sisupala's envy
summary: Sisupala insulted Krsna at the Rajasuya assembly; Krsna killed him, and he merged into the Lord's body.
lesson: Envy of the Lord is also thinking of Him, but without love.
useFor: Use for envy.

title: Duryodhana's greed
summary: Duryodhana would not return the Pandavas' share, not even enough land to put a needle point. Krsna's peace efforts failed and war began at Kurukshetra.
lesson: Greed destroys families.
useFor: Use for greed.

title: The Yaksha's questions to Yudhishthira
source: Mahabharata, Vana (Aranya) Parva, Sections CCCX–CCCXII, Yaksha-prasna (Ganguli tr.; not Prabhupada)
summary: Four Pandava brothers die drinking from a lake guarded by an unseen Yaksha, who asks Yudhishthira questions before he may drink. Asked what is most wonderful, Yudhishthira answers that day after day countless creatures go to the abode of Yama, yet those who remain believe themselves immortal. Because he chooses to revive Nakula, saying abstention from injury is the highest virtue, the Yaksha lets all his brothers live; the brothers rise and the hunger and thirst leave them (Section CCCXII).
lesson: Death is certain and the mind still lives as if immortal; the answer to that blindness is not clever argument but the path trod by the great devotees, which leads to Krishna.
useFor: Use to open the question of death and the soul (the "most wonderful" thing), then move to what Krishna says in BG 2.13 and 2.20: the soul does not die, so the real work is to prepare for the next life by bhakti. Yudhishthira himself is a devotee of Krishna, so the answer points to Him.

title: Bhishma on the bed of arrows praises Krishna
source: Mahabharata, Santi Parva (Rajadharmanusasana), Sections LI–LIV (Ganguli tr.; not Prabhupada)
summary: Krishna and the Pandavas come to Bhishma, who lies on a bed of arrows by the river Oghavati. Krishna asks if his mind is clear, and Bhishma, in pain, answers with a prayer: "Salutations to thee, O divine Krishna! Thou art the origin and thou art the dissolution of all the worlds." He asks Krishna to think of what would be good for himself, a devotee seeking His protection. Krishna replies that because Bhishma's devotion is very great, He has shown His celestial form.
lesson: At the hour of greatest suffering Bhishma's mind is fixed on Krishna; a devotee's real wealth is the remembrance of Krishna at death, and Krishna personally answers such devotion.
useFor: Use to show what a devotee thinks of at death, and prepare the audience to meet SB 1.9 (Bhishma's final prayers, already in the library as bhisma). Add it as a second witness from the Mahabharata.

title: Draupadi calls out to Krishna in the assembly
source: Mahabharata, Sabha Parva (Dyuta Parva), Section LXVI (Ganguli tr.; not Prabhupada)
summary: In the Kuru assembly Dussasana seizes Draupadi's garment and begins to drag it off before everyone. She cries "O Govinda, O thou who dwellest in Dwaraka, O Krishna... rescue me who am sinking in the Kaurava Ocean," and remembers Krishna. As her garment is pulled, clothes of many colours keep appearing, so that Dussasana tires and sits down while the kings applaud her.
lesson: When every human protector has failed, the devotee who calls only on Krishna is protected by Him; surrender means to cry out to Krishna without reservation.
useFor: Use under the surrender principle "Krishna will protect": place beside the six principles of surrender, and contrast the silent elders in the assembly with Draupadi, who turned to Krishna. Note the text itself says Dharma remained unseen and covered her; Draupadi called on Hari.

title: Karna gives away his armour and earrings
source: Mahabharata, Vana Parva (Kundalaharana), Sections CCXCIX–CCCVIII (Ganguli tr.; not Prabhupada)
summary: Surya warns Karna in a dream not to part with his natural armour and ear-rings when Indra begs for them. Karna refuses to be dissuaded, saying his fame is to be protected even with his life. When Indra comes disguised as a Brahmana, Karna offers land, women and cattle, then, recognising him, takes a dart in exchange and peels the mail from his body without any contortion of his face.
lesson: Karna's generosity is real and the Mahabharata honours it, but it served the side of Duryodhana; charity and honesty without Krishna do not make a person a devotee, while the same courage offered to Krishna would be perfection.
useFor: Use to separate morality from transcendental morality: admire Karna's vow, then ask what he served. Point to Indra's words in the text that "Krishna himself is protecting" Arjuna.

title: Karna refuses Krishna's offer
source: Mahabharata, Udyoga Parva (Bhagavad-yana), Sections 140–141 (Ganguli tr.; not Prabhupada)
summary: Krishna takes Karna on His chariot and tells him he is Kunti's son, urging him to join the Pandavas. Karna answers that he knows all this, but Adhiratha and Radha raised him, his wives and sons are bound to him, and Duryodhana made him chief antagonist of Arjuna. He says he cannot behave falsely towards Duryodhana "for the sake of death, or the ties of blood, or fear, or temptation", and asks Krishna to keep the talk secret.
lesson: Loyalty to a wrong association can close the door even when Krishna Himself stands at it; the company we promise ourselves to decides where we are taken.
useFor: Use under the power of association: ask who Karna is bound to and what happens when Krishna offers him another life. Contrast with Vibhisana (vibhisana-surrender), who left his brother for Rama.

title: Vidura's counsel to Dhritarashtra
source: Mahabharata, Udyoga Parva (Prajagara), Sections 33–40 (Ganguli tr.; not Prabhupada)
summary: Dhritarashtra cannot sleep, burning with worry about what Sanjaya will report from the Pandavas, and asks Vidura what is good for a sleepless man. Vidura answers that sleeplessness comes to a thief, a lustful person, one who has lost wealth, and the weak attacked by the strong, and goes on at length about conduct and virtue. The king listens and does not act on the advice.
lesson: Good advice from a devotee-minded elder is received and then ignored when the heart is attached; hearing without following leaves the ear full and the life unchanged.
useFor: Use under constructive criticism and hearing: ask what stopped Dhritarashtra. Bring in SB 1.13 (dhrtarastra, already in the library) where Vidura's teaching at last cuts the attachment.

title: Ekalavya and the guru's fee
source: Mahabharata, Adi Parva (Sambhava Parva), Section CXXXIV (Ganguli tr.; not Prabhupada)
summary: The Nishada prince Ekalavya is refused as a pupil by Drona, goes to the forest, makes a clay image of Drona and practises before it as if it were his real preceptor. His skill amazes the Pandavas, and when Drona asks for the thumb of his right hand as fee, he cuts it off cheerfully and gives it, but loses his former lightness of hand.
lesson: The pupil's faith in the guru is complete, but the story also warns: Drona's demand was driven by his own partiality. In Krishna consciousness the guru asks only what increases the disciple's service to Krishna, and the disciple's offering should be to that mission.
useFor: Use to discuss guru-bhakti and what a guru may rightly ask; keep the point on the guru as Krishna's representative rather than on the archer's skill.

title: Arjuna sees only the bird's head
source: Mahabharata, Adi Parva (Sambhava Parva), Section CXXXV (Ganguli tr.; not Prabhupada)
summary: Drona places a wooden bird on a tree and asks each pupil what he sees. Arjuna says he sees only the bird, then only the head of the vulture and not its body, and when told to shoot he strikes the head off. Drona embraces him.
lesson: The mind that sees one thing is fit for the work; in the same way, the mind that sees only Krishna in all engagements is fit for service. Arjuna's focus later becomes his choice to fight on Krishna's instruction (BG 18.73).
useFor: Use in concentration: show the scene, then say the same single-pointed mind is trained by hearing and chanting, and that Arjuna's greatest focus is "I will act according to Your instruction".

title: Hanuman humbles Bhima
source: Mahabharata, Vana Parva (Tirthayatra), Sections CXLV–CXLVII (Ganguli tr.; not Prabhupada)
summary: Bhima finds an old monkey blocking his path and asks him to move his tail. Bhima grasps the tail with his left hand, then both hands, and cannot lift it; he stands with a bashful face, bows with joined hands and asks forgiveness. The monkey is Hanuman, who tells of his service to Rama, that he asked to live as long as the story of Rama's deeds remains on earth, and Bhima bows to his elder brother.
lesson: Pride in one's own strength is dissolved in the presence of a pure servant of the Lord. The devotee prays to live as long as the Lord's story is heard.
useFor: Use for false ego and humility: show Bhima's strength failing against one old monkey who is Rama's servant, then Hanuman's own wish to live as long as Rama-katha is told.

title: King Sivi saves the dove
source: Mahabharata, Vana Parva (Markandeya-samasya), Section CXCVI [numbered CLXLVI in the scan] (Ganguli tr.; not Prabhupada)
summary: A pigeon takes shelter with King Sivi from a hawk. The hawk demands the pigeon as its food and, when offered a bull instead, asks for flesh of the king's thigh equal to the pigeon's weight. The king cuts off flesh but the pigeon still outweighs it, so he himself ascends the scale. The hawk and pigeon are revealed to be Indra and Agni, who came to test him.
lesson: The king gives up his own body rather than abandon one who has taken shelter; the Lord is even more firm to protect the surrendered devotee, as He promises in BG 18.66.
useFor: Use under surrender and protection: a king who refuses to give up a refugee. Compare with Krishna's promise "I shall deliver you from all sinful reactions".

title: Hanuman refuses to rest on his way to Lanka
source: Ramayana, Sundara Kanda (Book V), Canto I (Griffith verse tr., not Prabhupada)
summary: As Hanuman leaps over the ocean for Rama, the sea-god asks Mainaka to rise so he may rest. Mainaka offers rest and honour, but Hanuman answers "I may not rest; I must not stay or turn aside," touches the hill with his hand and flies on, with Rama's message as his only purpose.
lesson: The servant of Rama takes nothing, not even comfort, as an end in itself; every step is for the Lord's mission. Service does not stop for a pleasant resting-place.
useFor: Use for service attitude and steadiness: ask what "rest" Hanuman refuses and what resting-places tempt a devotee on the way to Krishna.

title: Bharata rules Ayodhya with Rama's sandals
source: Ramayana, Ayodhya Kanda (Book II), Canto CXII (Griffith verse tr., not Prabhupada)
summary: Bharata falls at Rama's feet asking him to return and rule. Rama will not break his father's word, so Bharata says he will wear hermit dress for fourteen seasons and "the rule and all affairs of state I to these shoes will delegate," promising to enter the fire if Rama does not return. The bright sandals are placed on his brow, bound on the elephant's head and carried back.
lesson: Bharata does not claim the throne as his own; he rules as the servant of the Lord's sandals. A devotee holds position and duty as Krishna's trust, not as ownership.
useFor: Use to teach the representative principle in guru-parampara: one governs as servant of the master's instruction.

title: Vibhisana leaves Ravana and takes shelter of Rama
source: Ramayana, Yuddha Kanda (Book VI), Canto XVII (Griffith verse tr., not Prabhupada)
summary: Vibhisana tells Ravana to return Sita and is spurned "like a base-born slave." He leaves his wife and children, flies to Rama's side of the sea and announces himself to Sugriva: "I pray thee... speed to him who saves in hour of need, and tell him... that suppliant here Vibhishan stands." Sugriva carries the news to Rama.
lesson: Surrender requires leaving what opposes service to the Lord, even family and home, and the Lord receives one who comes with sincere shelter; Vibhisana's act answers Karna's opposite choice.
useFor: Use with the six principles of surrender, "to accept what favours service and reject what does not", and contrast with karna-loyalty.

title: Sabari welcomes Rama
source: Ramayana, Aranya Kanda (Book III), Canto LXXV (Griffith verse tr., not Prabhupada)
summary: Rama and Lakshmana come to the hermitage of the aged Savari near Pampa. She meets them with raised hands, bows, and gives water for their lips and feet. She says, "My penance meed this day I see complete, my lord, in meeting thee," shows them the grove of the saints she had served, and asks leave to give up her body to join them.
lesson: A long life of simple service to the saints bears its fruit in the Lord's presence; the Lord looks at the love, not at the status.
useFor: Use for spontaneous devotion and gratitude: a poor, old woman whose whole life was service to the sages receives the Lord Himself.

title: Jatayu fights Ravana for Sita
source: Ramayana, Aranya Kanda (Book III), Cantos L and LXIX (Griffith verse tr., not Prabhupada)
summary: Awakened by Sita's cries, the old vulture Jatayu warns Ravana to keep to the law, saying that no king may touch another's wife. In the fight his wings are cut. Rama finds him dying, hears that Ravana took Sita south, and lays him on a pyre, performs the rites that the soul may find free passage, and pours libations in the Godavari.
lesson: The Lord honours the servant who gives his life for His service as His own family; Rama performs the funeral rites Himself.
useFor: Use for dedication to a higher cause: an old, weak devotee does what he can for the Lord's consort and is rewarded by the Lord personally.

title: Manthara poisons Kaikeyi's mind
source: Ramayana, Ayodhya Kanda (Book II), Cantos VII–IX (Griffith verse tr., not Prabhupada)
summary: The hunchbacked maid Manthara sees Ayodhya decorated for Rama's consecration. Over three cantos she persuades Queen Kaikeyi to recall two boons from the king, to demand "twice seven years of banishment" for Rama and the throne for Bharata.
lesson: Bad association with a clever, envious adviser can turn a queen who loved Rama into the cause of His exile; the ear that listens to one who envies the Lord's devotees is led away from Him.
useFor: Use for association and asat-sanga: a short, concrete story of how one voice changed a decision in one night.

title: Jada Bharata and King Rahugana
summary: King Rahugana, going to Kapila, presses the silent Jada Bharata into carrying his palanquin, and rebukes him when the carrying is uneven. Jada Bharata answers with the teaching of the self and the body, and the king, realising he has offended a great soul, falls at his feet and asks pardon. In 5.12.12 Jada Bharata tells the king that the Absolute Truth is realised only by the mercy of a great devotee: not by celibacy, household rules, vanaprastha, sannyasa or severe austerities.
lesson: A pure devotee may look like a fool, yet his dust is the way to the Absolute Truth; real knowledge comes by humbly receiving the mercy of a Vaisnava, not by status or austerity alone.
useFor: Use under Vaisnava aparadha and humility: the king was learned and powerful, and still insulted a great soul; show the verse as the reply that follows his fall at the devotee's feet.

title: Jagai and Madhai are delivered
source: Madhurya-kadambini (Visvanatha Cakravarti Thakura, tr. 2018), account of the Jagai-Madhai pastime; the pastime is told in Caitanya-bhagavata Madhya 13 and in CC (not Prabhupada; reference to be confirmed)
summary: Mahaprabhu sends Nityananda and Haridasa Thakura from door to door to ask everyone to chant Krishna's names. They meet the drunkards Jagai and Madhai, brahmanas by birth who also looted and murdered, and Madhai strikes Nityananda's head with a shard of a broken pot. When Mahaprabhu calls for His discus, Nityananda says Jagai saved Him, Mahaprabhu embraces Jagai, and Madhai, after Nityananda's prayer, also receives krsna-prema and dances chanting "Hare Krsna".
lesson: The holy name and the mercy of Nityananda reach even the most fallen; no one is excluded, and the deliverer asks only that the offender be forgiven.
useFor: Use to answer the misconception that ISKCON is for the select or perfect: the Lord's most intimate associate received blows to give the name. Also the power of the holy name for habits.

title: Sankhacuda, Sudama's demon birth, and Siva's spear
source: Brahma-vaivarta Purana, Prakrti-khanda, chapters XVII–XX in Sen's translation (Sen 1920; not Prabhupada)
summary: Sudama, cursed in Goloka, is told he will be born as a demon and will come back to Goloka in half a moment, which is a manvantara on earth. As the demon Sankhacuda, protected by an amulet, he is attacked by Siva with a spear given by Visnu. Visnu begs the amulet from him as an old Brahmana, and when Siva casts the spear the demon puts down his bow, meditates, remembers Hari, and is reduced to ashes. He then takes a cowherd's form with a flute, goes to Goloka, and is taken on Radha and Krishna's lap.
lesson: Even the demon who dies remembering Hari reaches Goloka; the Lord's plans and a devotee's curse are both used to bring the servant back to Him.
useFor: Use with the Sankhacuda-Tulasi conversation topic (bss-50): the text of the curse and return, then Tulasi's own story (tulasi-sankhacuda).

title: Tulasi, Sankhacuda's wife, and Hari's boon
source: Brahma-vaivarta Purana, Prakrti-khanda, chapters XXI–XXII in Sen's translation (Sen 1920; not Prabhupada)
summary: Hari takes the form of Sankhacuda and approaches Tulsi. She curses Hari with a heart of stone, saying he will be worshipped in the world as a stone, and Hari answers that by her curse he will become a stone on the Gandaki; he blesses her to become the holy basil, whose flowers and leaves will be offered in His worship and whose leaf, offered, is more pleasing than a thousand jars of honey.
lesson: Tulasi becomes the permanent servant at the Lord's feet; to offer a tulasi leaf is itself an act of devotion and brings the Lord's pleasure. The stone form is the Salagrama-sila.
useFor: Use for tulasi-seva and Deity worship: the story gives the Puranic source of tulasi and salagrama worship. Pair with BG 9.26 (leaf, flower, fruit or water).
